clue.text: Hairstyle commemorating Yorkist victory?

definitions.meaning: in rhyming slang, ... Fair stands for hair, so the word is slang for a head of hair
the Yorkists won the Battle of ... in 1471, during the Wars of the Roses

explanation.surface: A haircut named to celebrate a battle won by the House of York.
explanation.walkthrough: Barnet is a town north of London; 'barnet' is Cockney rhyming slang (Barnet Fair = hair).
explanation.definitionFit: Rhyming slang turns the town's fair into a word for hair, and the town also names a famous Wars of the Roses battle.

clue.text: Blue Boar Mystery to attack political slogan?

indicators.note: a mystery is a puzzle, so the letters of the inn name are jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: A detective story set at the Blue Boar inn, read as a party's campaign slogan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'political slogan?' is a cryptic extra: split the answer as BE LABOUR, an imagined election cry.
explanation.definitionFit: To belabour someone is to beat or assail them, physically or with words.

clue.text: The Last Emperor (and city founder)

definitions.meaning: ... Augustulus was the last emperor of the Western Roman Empire, deposed in 476
the legendary twin who founded Rome after killing his brother Remus

explanation.surface: A film title paired with the founder of a city.
explanation.definitionFit: Both the final western ruler of Rome and the mythical builder of the city bore this name.

clue.text: Maybe some other place in Oz

definitions.text: Maybe some other place in Oz

parts.words: Maybe some other place in Oz
parts.note: a word for any other location, playfully linked to the land of Oz as a faraway somewhere

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a place might be found in Oz, or Australia.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means in or to some other place, a fit description of the imaginary land beyond the rainbow.

clue.text: She went for gold in the race, but finished with only the silver

definitions.text: She went for gold in the race, but finished with only the silver

parts.words: She went for gold in the race, but finished with only the silver
parts.note: a Greek huntress who stooped to pick up golden apples during a footrace and so lost it

explanation.surface: An athlete chasing a gold medal who ends up in second place.
explanation.walkthrough: The gold is Hippomenes's golden apples, not a medal; 'silver' is the second place she finished in.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the swift huntress lost her race to Hippomenes after stopping for three golden apples.

clue.text: Du Maurier's model character

parts.note: George du Maurier wrote an 1894 novel about a young artist's model hypnotised by Svengali

explanation.surface: A model figure from a du Maurier novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'model' means an artist's model, not an exemplary person; the heroine also gave her name to a hat.
explanation.definitionFit: The title heroine of George du Maurier's novel poses for painters in Paris.

clue.text: Roy Campbell's was on a dark horse

definitions.text: Roy Campbell's was on a dark horse

parts.words: Roy Campbell's was on a dark horse
parts.note: the South African poet titled his 1951 autobiography with a phrase about a dark horse

explanation.surface: Something belonging to the poet Roy Campbell rested on a dark horse.
explanation.walkthrough: Roy Campbell's memoir is called Light on a Dark Horse.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing first word of Campbell's memoir title is the opposite of darkness.

clue.text: Clemency is associated with Dickens's

parts.note: Clemency is a servant in Dickens's Christmas book The Battle of Life, given a surname here

explanation.surface: Mercy is a quality associated with Dickens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clemency' looks like the virtue but is a character's first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Clemency's surname in Dickens's story The Battle of Life completes the clue.

clue.text: Aircraftman Lawrence, so-called to give a sort of clue

parts.note: AC is the RAF abbreviation for Aircraftman
T. E. Lawrence enlisted in the RAF under the assumed name John Hume Ross

explanation.surface: T. E. Lawrence serving under an alias, as material for a puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: Crossword clues come in two directions, and this is one of them, opposite to down.

clue.text: Royalty on steam train in Edwin Drood

parts.note: a princess is a member of royalty
puffer is a childish name for a steam locomotive

explanation.surface: A royal riding a steam locomotive in a Dickens novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The character runs an opium den in Dickens's unfinished The Mystery of Edwin Drood.
explanation.definitionFit: The opium-den keeper in Dickens's last novel is known by this nickname.

clue.text: It is for the use of highly placed priests

definitions.text: It is for the use of highly placed priests

parts.words: It is for the use of highly placed priests
parts.note: a building for Tibetan monks, 'highly placed' because the monasteries sit high in the Himalaya, not because the clergy are senior

explanation.surface: Something reserved for senior clergy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'highly placed' suggests rank, but means altitude: Tibetan monasteries in the mountains.
explanation.definitionFit: A Tibetan Buddhist monastery houses lamas, the monks and priests of that tradition.

clue.text: Friend of Chaucer from Welsh coastal area

definitions.meaning: John ..., the medieval poet, to whom Chaucer dedicated Troilus and Criseyde
a peninsula west of Swansea in south Wales

explanation.surface: A companion of Chaucer who came from the Welsh coast.
explanation.definitionFit: The poet John Gower, Chaucer's 'moral' friend, shares his surname with the Welsh peninsula.

clue.text: What he wrote seems to have been just above his head

definitions.text: What he wrote seems to have been just above his head

parts.words: What he wrote seems to have been just above his head
parts.note: the American novelist James wrote the 1979 novel Just Above My Head

explanation.surface: A writer whose work was beyond his own understanding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'just above his head' sounds like 'too hard for him', but is his novel's title, Just Above My Head.
explanation.definitionFit: James, the American author of Just Above My Head, has this surname.

clue.text: However, lots apply for part in pantomime

parts.note: however means but
tons means lots, a great quantity

explanation.surface: Many people audition for a pantomime role.
explanation.walkthrough: Pantomime is a British Christmas stage show; in Cinderella the page boy is called Buttons.
explanation.definitionFit: The cheerful page boy in the pantomime Cinderella is a stock role.

clue.text: Off with thy liquor / Drink-s out, and a fig for the vicar (Scott, Lady of the Lake)

definitions.text: Off with thy liquor / Drink-s out, and a fig for the vicar (Scott, Lady of the Lake)

parts.words: Off with thy liquor / Drink-s out, and a fig for the vicar (Scott, Lady of the Lake)
parts.note: a quotation with a gap after 'Drink': fill it with the old word for 'in the manner of', as in drinking deep Dutch-fashion

explanation.surface: A soldier's drinking song from Scott's poem, with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: Scott's line reads 'Drink upsees out'; the word means heavily, in the Dutch or Frisian manner.
explanation.definitionFit: The old word, from Dutch op zijn, means in the fashion of, used of drinking deeply.

clue.text: Old race recalled in strange ode on small children

indicators.note: strange signals that the little word ode is to be scrambled

parts.note: mites are small children

explanation.surface: An ancient people remembered in an odd poem about little ones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strange' rearranges ODE to EDO.
explanation.definitionFit: The descendants of Esau, a people of the Old Testament, form an ancient nation.

clue.text: Dictum pitied six in trouble

indicators.note: letters in trouble are in disorder, so they get rearranged

explanation.surface: A pronouncement that pitied six people who were in difficulties.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin for 'he himself said it', an assertion resting only on the speaker's authority.

clue.text: Griskin was not, Eliot observed

parts.note: in Whispers of Immortality, T. S. Eliot describes Grishkin's friendly bust as ...

explanation.surface: A remark by Eliot about what Griskin was not.
explanation.walkthrough: Eliot's poem says of Grishkin 'Uncorseted, her friendly bust'.
explanation.definitionFit: Wearing a stiff laced undergarment is what Eliot says Grishkin went without.

clue.text: Some magic in eastern movies for film buff

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Some oriental magic in films for a cinema lover.
explanation.definitionFit: A devotee of the cinema, from the French word for a film enthusiast.

clue.text: Fabulous wolf is oriental and forbidding

parts.note: E is short for eastern, oriental
grim means forbidding, stern

explanation.surface: A wolf of fable described as eastern and menacing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fabulous' means from a fable: the wolf in the Reynard the Fox stories.
explanation.definitionFit: The wolf enemy of Reynard in medieval beast fables bears this name.

clue.text: Reservation by Waldo Frank?

definitions.meaning: a saving clause or mental reservation, as in a qualifying condition
the American writer Waldo Frank published a book of essays called ... in 1924

explanation.surface: A booking made by the writer Waldo Frank.
explanation.definitionFit: A proviso or excuse, and the singular of the title of Frank's essay collection.

clue.text: William Styron did it in darkness

definitions.text: William Styron did it in darkness

parts.words: William Styron did it in darkness
parts.note: William Styron's first novel was ... in Darkness, 1951

explanation.surface: Something the novelist William Styron did with the lights off.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening words of Styron's novel title Lie Down in Darkness.
explanation.definitionFit: To recline flat is the action named in the first words of Styron's title.

clue.text: Snow reported, novel business

definitions.meaning: C. P. Snow's novel The ..., in his Strangers and Brothers sequence
a matter or concern, as in 'that's my own business'

explanation.surface: Weather news of snowfall, a fresh piece of business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snow' is the novelist C. P. Snow, not weather.
explanation.definitionFit: C. P. Snow's 1960 novel has this title, and the word also means a matter or concern.

clue.text: UN free a troublesome American poet

indicators.note: troublesome letters are unruly, so they are put in a new order

explanation.surface: Freeing a difficult poet via the United Nations.
explanation.definitionFit: Philip Freneau was an 18th-century American poet, known as the poet of the Revolution.

clue.text: Triumph in Wessex cello sonata ()

indicators.note: in shows the answer sits inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A triumphant cello sonata performance in Wessex.
explanation.walkthrough: Wessex is Hardy's name for south-west England; the answer spans wesSEX CELlo.
explanation.definitionFit: To excel is to triumph, to outdo others.

clue.text: Poles hold German poet

indicators.note: hold means the poles enclose the abbreviation for German

parts.note: rods are poles

explanation.surface: Polish people harbouring a German poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poles' looks like people from Poland but means rods. The poet is W. R. Rodgers of Northern Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: W. R. Rodgers was a Northern Irish poet of the mid-20th century.

clue.text: Composer from chateau, richly appointed ()

indicators.note: from shows the answer is drawn out of the letters of the following words

explanation.surface: A composer from a lavishly furnished chateau.
explanation.definitionFit: Georges Auric was a French composer, one of Les Six.

clue.text: Eliot showed happy Roman cat at lair

parts.note: felix is Latin for happy and the name of a cartoon cat
a holt is an animal's lair, especially an otter's

explanation.surface: Eliot displayed a cheerful cat from Rome at its den.
explanation.walkthrough: George Eliot's novel Felix Holt, the Radical (1866).
explanation.definitionFit: George Eliot wrote a novel named after its radical hero, so the title stands for her work.

clue.text: Johnson's roses?

parts.note: Samuel Johnson ran a periodical, The Rambler; a climbing kind of rose shares the name

explanation.surface: Roses grown by Dr Johnson.
explanation.walkthrough: Johnson wrote the essays of The Rambler; rambler roses are climbing roses.
explanation.definitionFit: Climbing roses are called by the same name as Johnson's periodical essays.

clue.text: So heaven, shall dying Greece restore (Pope, Iliad)

definitions.text: So heaven, shall dying Greece restore (Pope, Iliad)

parts.words: So heaven, shall dying Greece restore (Pope, Iliad)
parts.note: a line from Pope's Iliad with a word missing after 'heaven,': fill in the past participle meaning appeased

explanation.surface: A quotation from Pope's translation of Homer, with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: Pope's line runs 'So heaven, atoned, shall dying Greece restore'.
explanation.definitionFit: Appeased or reconciled, a heaven made amends to is the sense Pope needs.
